description: Hi. I am Jiwoo, and I am the creator of this small campaign, " Operation the Last Night". In this game, you would be able to find yourself building a spacecraft for your mission. Also, you would find various challenges and obstacles along the way. Thank you for playing, and I hope you have fun. Also, I am not looking for any team members. ありがとうございます
summary:
Operation Last Light is a browser game that teaches how real space missions are designed. A meteor is five minutes from impact, and players have one spacecraft and a two-minute launch window to build a tracker that can pin down where it will land.

Players choose one of three missions: Earth Watch, Lunar Relay or Deep Scout. They then build the spacecraft from real trade-offs: orbit, bus, battery, instruments, antenna and launch vehicle. A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, data and lifetime, and nothing launches while any of them is red. After liftoff, players fly five hands-on tasks unique to their mission, such as a gravity-assist slingshot or surviving the lunar night. A post-mission report then explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

Mission design is usually taught through dry tables. Here, players learn engineering trade-offs by making them, and every mistake shows its consequence. That makes systems thinking easy for students and newcomers to grasp. The game runs in any browser and needs no installation. A team mode lets up to four players share the design.
details: Operation Last Light is a browser game that teaches space mission design through play. Players choose one of three missions (Earth Watch, Lunar Relay or Deep Scout), each with its own budget, science target and allowed orbits. With a two-minute launch window, they build a spacecraft by picking an orbit, bus, battery, instruments, antenna and launch vehicle, while a live dashboard calculates mass, power, budget, data downlink and lifetime. If any system is red, the launch is locked. After liftoff, players complete five interactive tasks unique to their mission, 15 in all, such as a gravity-assist slingshot, surviving the lunar night or clearing Martian dust from solar panels. Their design choices shape each task, and a post-mission report explains exactly why the mission succeeded or failed. The game helps students and newcomers understand that engineering is about trade-offs, where improving one system always costs another, and we hope it sparks interest in aerospace and STEM. Because it is free, needs no installation and runs on any computer, tablet or phone, it works well in classrooms, and Team mode turns it into a group exercise in negotiation, with each player holding a secret priority. We built it in HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks, using the Canvas 2D API and SVG for graphics. We developed it with the help of Claude, an AI coding assistant, used Playwright for automated balance testing, and host it on GitHub and Vercel. What makes it creative is that real engineering concepts are wrapped in a disaster story with a ticking clock, a mission-control crew that reacts to every choice, and endings that depend on how well you design and fly. Throughout, we balanced realism with fun, made sure every mission can be won, and kept it accessible with light and dark themes, touch support, text labels alongside colours and plain-language feedback. We also built in replayability, and treated failure as a chance to learn, with a “Redesign & retry” button on every result.
